date-input.what: A form field for choosing one calendar date, usually with a pop-up calendar picker. It keeps dates in a consistent format.
uses: Setting a deadline, due date or report date.
Booking an appointment or delivery day.
Filtering a list by a single day.
avoid: Birth dates or dates far in the past: separate day, month and year fields are faster to type.
A start and end together: use a date range picker.
practices: Label the field with what the date means, not with the format.
Set minimum and maximum dates when only some days are allowed.
Prefill a likely default, such as today.
Explain the accepted range in help text.

time-input.what: A form field for entering a time of day, in hours and minutes. Browsers show it in the user's 12 or 24-hour style.
uses: Choosing a start or end time for an event.
Setting opening hours.
Picking a time for a reminder.
avoid: A length of time, like 90 minutes: use a duration field.
A full date and time together: use a date-time field.
practices: Use a sensible step, such as 15 minutes, to avoid awkward values.
Show the timezone when users may be in a different one.
Label the field clearly, for example 'Starts at'.
Validate that end times come after start times.

datetime-input.what: A single form field for choosing a date and a time together. It captures one exact moment without needing two separate controls.
uses: Scheduling when a task or message should run.
Setting when a link or offer expires.
Recording when an incident happened.
avoid: A start and end: use two fields side by side.
Only a date or only a time: use the simpler field.
practices: State which timezone the value uses, as the field itself holds none.
Label it with the event, such as 'Start run at'.
Set limits so users cannot pick impossible moments.
Test on phones, where pickers differ from desktop.

duration-input.what: A form field for entering a length of time, such as hours and minutes. Separate labelled parts make the unit clear.
uses: Setting how long a shift or meeting lasts.
Choosing how long data is kept.
Setting a reminder offset, like 15 minutes before.
avoid: A specific time of day: use a time field.
A short fixed list of lengths: use a select.
practices: Show the unit next to each number.
Accept values like 90 minutes and tidy them into 1 h 30 min.
Set sensible minimum and maximum values.
Show the total in plain words after entry.

timezone-select.what: A dropdown for choosing a timezone, usually listed by region or city name. It makes sure times mean the same to everyone.
uses: Setting a user's profile timezone.
Setting the timezone of a site, team or event.
Showing a meeting time to people in different regions.
avoid: When the browser's timezone is enough: detect it instead of asking.
Choosing a country or language: those are separate settings.
practices: Preselect a likely zone from the user's profile or browser.
List places by name, such as Europe/Paris, not only offsets.
Store the zone name, not a fixed offset, so daylight saving works.
Make long lists searchable.

weekday-toggle.what: A row of seven buttons for choosing days of the week. People switch each day on or off in place.
uses: Choosing which days a task or event repeats.
Setting opening days or working days.
Selecting days for alerts or reports.
avoid: Picking one single day of the week: use a select or radio buttons.
Picking specific dates: use a calendar.
practices: Start the week on the day the user's region uses.
Offer shortcuts like 'Weekdays' and 'Every day'.
Show selected days with more than colour alone.
Give each toggle its full day name for screen readers.

recurrence-select.what: A dropdown of common repeat patterns, like daily or weekly, with a custom option for more detailed rules.
uses: Making an event or task repeat.
Scheduling a recurring report or export.
Setting up repeating bookings or reminders.
avoid: A one-off event: do not show repeat options.
Very complex schedules only: use a dedicated schedule editor.
practices: Show the actual day in options, such as 'Weekly on Thursday'.
Put 'Does not repeat' first as the default.
Reveal extra fields only when 'Custom' is chosen.
Let users set when the repeat ends.

reminder-select.what: A dropdown for choosing how long before an event a reminder is sent. It offers common lead times in one short list.
uses: Reminding people before an appointment or meeting.
Warning ahead of a task deadline.
Setting alerts for bookings or renewals.
avoid: Exact reminder times unrelated to an event: use a date-time field.
Urgent alerts that need no setup: send them directly.
practices: Offer a short list of common lead times.
Include 'No reminder' and 'At time of event'.
Remember the user's last choice as the default.
Allow more than one reminder per event.

day-number.what: The number of the day within a month, shown in a calendar cell or date badge, such as 6 or 23.
uses: Showing each day in a month calendar.
Labelling small date badges on cards or lists.
Building mini calendars in date pickers.
avoid: Showing a full date: write the whole date in words instead.
Showing the day of the week: use the weekday name.
practices: Align numbers in columns so they are easy to scan.
Leave out the leading zero.
Add the full date in markup for assistive technology.
Keep the size consistent across cells.

weekday-name.what: The name of a day of the week, short in column headers (Mon) or in full in lists (Monday).
uses: Heading the columns of a calendar.
Labelling rows in an agenda or schedule.
Writing dates in a readable way, like 'Friday 6 November'.
avoid: Where the date number alone is clear.
Long text where full words fit: avoid cryptic abbreviations.
practices: Use short forms only where space is tight.
Keep abbreviations consistent across the page.
Follow the user's language and locale.
Provide the full name in a title or label.

month-name.what: The name of a month, often with its year, used as a heading for a calendar or a group of dated items.
uses: Heading a calendar view.
Separating groups in an agenda or timeline.
Labelling a month in a report or archive.
avoid: Showing exact dates: use a full date instead.
Very short space: a short month form or number may fit better.
practices: Show the year when it is not the current one.
Spell out the month to avoid day-month confusion.
Use a real heading so people can navigate.
Follow the user's language.

year-label.what: The year shown as a small, quiet label next to a month or as the heading of a yearly view.
uses: Showing the year beside a month name.
Heading a year view or archive.
Marking dates that fall outside the current year.
avoid: When the year is obvious from context: leave it out.
Showing a complete date: write the whole date together.
practices: Keep it less prominent than the month or day.
Use four digits to avoid confusion.
Show it when the year is not the current one.
Keep it right next to what it describes.

week-number.what: The number of a week within the year, such as W45. Some regions and teams plan by week number.
uses: Showing week numbers beside month calendar rows.
Heading weeks in a planning view.
Naming sprints, shifts or production weeks.
avoid: Audiences who do not use week numbers: use a date range instead.
Exact days matter: show real dates.
practices: Say which numbering system is used, such as ISO weeks.
Mark it clearly as a week number, for example W45.
Show it only where the audience uses it.
Pair it with a date range when space allows.

time-label.what: A time of day written as text, such as 08:30 or 8:30 AM, in the format the reader is used to.
uses: Showing when an event starts or ends.
Labelling hours on a day view.
Timestamps in logs and activity lists.
avoid: Recent events where 'ago' reads better: use a relative time.
A length of time: use a duration label.
practices: Follow the reader's 12 or 24-hour habit.
Align times in columns so they are easy to scan.
Write ranges with an en dash, like 08:30–10:00.
Show the timezone when it may differ.

date-label.what: A date written out for people to read, such as 6 November 2026 or Fri 6 Nov.
uses: Showing due dates, publish dates or event dates.
Labelling rows in tables and lists.
Showing when something was created or changed.
avoid: Recent events where '2 minutes ago' reads better: use a relative time.
Input of a date: use a date field.
practices: Spell out the month to avoid confusion between day and month.
Use shorter forms only in dense tables.
Follow the reader's language and locale.
Mark up the exact date for machines and screen readers.

relative-time.what: A time written as how long ago or from now it is, such as '2 minutes ago' or 'in 3 days'.
uses: Activity feeds and comments.
'Last seen' and 'last updated' labels.
Notifications and recent changes.
avoid: Logs, audit trails and legal records: show exact times.
Dates far from now: show the full date.
practices: Show the exact time on hover or in a tooltip.
Switch to a full date after about a week.
Keep the text fresh as time passes.
Make the exact time available to screen readers.

timezone-label.what: A short label, such as CET or UTC+1, that tells readers which timezone a time is in.
uses: Showing meeting times to people in different places.
Labelling a site's opening hours.
Showing times in shared schedules and logs.
avoid: When everyone is in one zone and it is obvious: leave it out.
Choosing a zone: use a timezone select.
practices: Place it right next to the time.
Give the full zone name in a tooltip.
Use a familiar abbreviation or UTC offset.
Be consistent across the page.

duration-label.what: A length of time written in short form, such as 45 min, 1 h 30 min or 3 d.
uses: Showing how long an event or task lasts.
Showing time spent in tables and reports.
Labelling video or audio length.
avoid: A point in time: use a date or time label.
Entering a duration: use a duration field.
practices: Use short, consistent units.
Avoid mixed styles like 90 minutes and 1.5h.
Skip zero parts, such as '0 min'.
Include a machine-readable value for assistive tools.

countdown-label.what: A label that shows the time left until a moment and updates as it runs down.
uses: Showing when a session is about to expire.
Holding a booking or basket for a limited time.
Counting down to the start of an event.
avoid: Distant dates: show the date instead.
Pressure tactics: avoid fake urgency.
practices: Show a correct starting value without relying on scripts.
Do not announce every second to screen readers.
Make it look more urgent only near the end.
Say what happens when it reaches zero.

today-marker.what: A visual mark that highlights the current day in a calendar so people can find 'now' quickly.
uses: Highlighting today in a month grid.
Marking today in mini calendars and date pickers.
Orienting people in a schedule.
avoid: Marking a chosen day: use a selected-day marker.
Marking events: use an event dot or bar.
practices: Mark only one day per view.
Use shape or weight as well as colour.
Tell screen readers it is the current date.
Keep it different from the selected-day style.

selected-day-marker.what: A visual mark showing which calendar day or range the user has chosen.
uses: Showing the chosen date in a date picker.
Marking the start and end of a date range.
Showing the active day in a calendar view.
avoid: Marking today: use a today marker.
Showing days with events: use event dots.
practices: Use a strong fill that stands out from other days.
Do not rely on colour alone.
Tell screen readers which day is selected.
Make today and selected states look different.

outside-day-marker.what: A style for days that belong to the previous or next month but appear in a month grid to complete full weeks.
uses: Filling the first and last weeks of a month grid.
Letting people jump to a neighbouring month.
Keeping calendar rows a regular length.
avoid: Days that are unavailable: use a disabled style.
Days with no real meaning: leave the cells empty.
practices: Mute them so the current month stands out.
Keep them readable and keep enough contrast.
Let them open their own month when clicked.
Label them clearly for screen readers.

weekend-marker.what: A light tint or style that sets weekend days apart from weekdays in calendars and schedules.
uses: Month grids and week views.
Gantt charts and resource schedulers.
Date pickers where weekends matter.
avoid: Days that are closed or unavailable: use a holiday or off marker.
Locales with different weekends: do not hard-code Saturday and Sunday.
practices: Keep the tint subtle so events stay clear.
Follow the user's local weekend days.
Do not use colour as the only cue where it matters.
Keep contrast for text on the tint.

holiday-marker.what: A mark on calendar days that are public holidays or closure days, often with the holiday name.
uses: Showing public holidays in a calendar.
Marking days a business is closed.
Warning that a date may be unavailable.
avoid: Ordinary weekends: use a weekend marker.
Events: use event markers.
practices: Show the holiday name, not just a colour.
Combine tint with a shape or underline.
Say the holiday in labels for screen readers.
Let users hide holidays they do not need.

event-dot.what: A small dot in a calendar cell that shows a day has events, or colour-codes an event's calendar.
uses: Showing which days have events in a mini calendar.
Colour-coding calendars in an agenda.
Saving space where full event titles do not fit.
avoid: Showing event details: use an event bar or a list.
Many events per day: show a count instead.
practices: Make the day's events one tap away.
Say 'has events' in the day's label.
Do not use colour as the only key.
Keep dots few and spaced clearly.

event-bar.what: A horizontal block in a calendar that shows one timed event with its title and time.
uses: Showing events in month, week and day views.
Showing meetings and appointments.
Showing bookings in a resource schedule.
avoid: Events that last all day or several days: use an all-day bar.
A quick sign that a day has events: use a dot.
practices: Show the time and title.
Truncate long titles and give the full title on hover.
Mark tentative or cancelled events with more than colour.
Keep text readable on the tint.

allday-bar.what: A bar that spans the width of a day or several days to show an event with no set time.
uses: Showing all-day events in a week view.
Showing events that span several days.
Showing trade fairs, holidays or trips.
avoid: Events with a start and end time: use an event bar.
Single marks on a day: use a dot.
practices: Use a solid fill so it stands apart from timed events.
Show arrow ends when it continues past the view.
Keep the title readable.
Group all-day bars in their own row.

hour-gridline.what: A faint horizontal line across a day or week view that marks each hour, with a time label.
uses: Giving scale to day and week views.
Resource and room schedulers.
Helping people place events at the right time.
avoid: Views that are not time-based: do not add lines.
Very dense schedules: avoid heavy lines.
practices: Keep lines light so events stand out.
Label each hour in the side margin.
Use a dashed or lighter line for half hours.
Keep spacing consistent.

now-indicator.what: A line across a day or week view that shows the current time and moves as time passes.
uses: Showing the present in a day or week view.
Showing progress along a timeline.
Helping people find what is happening now.
avoid: Views that show only past or future dates: do not show it.
Showing a deadline: use a deadline marker.
practices: Make it clearly different from events and gridlines.
Use shape as well as colour, such as a line with a dot.
Update it every minute.
Scroll to it when the view opens.

availability-color.what: A set of marks that show whether time slots or people are free, busy, tentative or away.
uses: Showing when people or rooms are available.
Offering free slots for booking.
Comparing availability across many people.
avoid: Showing events themselves: use event bars.
Only free versus busy: fewer states may be clearer.
practices: Use patterns or labels as well as colour.
Provide a legend that explains each state.
Name the state in each slot's label.
Keep the number of states small.

priority-marker.what: A small mark that shows how important a task, ticket or alert is, such as low, medium, high or urgent.
uses: Ranking tasks in lists and boards.
Showing urgency on support tickets.
Sorting alerts by importance.
avoid: Showing progress or status: use a status badge.
Items that are all the same importance: do not mark them.
practices: Use a word as well as an icon or colour.
Make levels clearly different in shape or size.
Keep the scale short, with four levels at most.
Use the same scale everywhere.

deadline-marker.what: A mark that shows when something is due, usually a flag icon with the date.
uses: Showing due dates on tasks.
Marking deadlines on plans and timelines.
Warning that a due date is close.
avoid: Showing something already late: use an overdue marker.
Showing a completed date: use a plain date label.
practices: Show the date next to the flag.
Change the look when the deadline is close.
Use words like 'Due tomorrow' for close dates.
Do not rely on colour alone.

overdue-marker.what: A strong mark that shows something has passed its due date, ideally saying how late it is.
uses: Marking late tasks and invoices.
Highlighting missed deadlines in a list.
Prompting people to act on late work.
avoid: Items not yet due: use a deadline marker.
Items that are finished: show them as done.
practices: Say how late it is, such as 'Overdue by 2 days'.
Combine colour with an icon and words.
Keep it distinct but not alarming for minor delays.
Remove it once the item is done.

milestone-marker.what: A diamond-shaped mark on a plan or timeline that shows a key point or achievement.
uses: Marking key dates on roadmaps.
Showing phases on Gantt charts.
Tracking project stages.
avoid: Regular tasks with a length: use a bar.
Single deadlines on a task: use a deadline marker.
practices: Show state with fill or outline, not colour alone.
Name each milestone in text.
State whether it is done, upcoming or missed.
Use the diamond shape consistently.

drag-handle.what: A small grip control that lets people pick up an item and move it, often to reorder a list.
uses: Reordering list rows or cards.
Moving events in a schedule.
Moving cards between board columns.
avoid: Items that never move: do not add a handle.
As the only way to reorder: also offer buttons or keys.
practices: Offer a keyboard or button alternative to dragging.
Make the handle large enough to grab.
Show that the item is lifted while dragging.
Announce moves to screen readers.

resize-handle.what: A grip on the edge of an item or panel that lets people drag to change its size or length.
uses: Changing the length of an event in a calendar.
Resizing side panels or columns.
Adjusting the length of bars in a Gantt chart.
avoid: Precise values: offer a field to type them.
Items with a fixed size: do not add a handle.
practices: Show the new value while resizing.
Snap to sensible steps, such as 15 minutes.
Offer a keyboard or form alternative.
Make the grip big enough to reach easily.

planning-icons.what: A set of small pictures for time and scheduling ideas, such as calendar, clock, repeat, reminder and deadline.
uses: Labelling date and time fields and buttons.
Marking reminders, repeats and deadlines.
Adding quick cues in calendars and task lists.
avoid: Replacing a clear word when meaning could be missed.
Decoration with no meaning.
practices: Use one icon for one idea everywhere.
Pair icons with words where space allows.
Give icon-only buttons an accessible name.
Keep size and weight consistent.

bar-chart.what: A chart that compares values across categories using bars of different lengths. Bars can be vertical or horizontal.
uses: Comparing amounts across categories.
Showing values over a few time periods.
Ranking items from largest to smallest.
avoid: Many time points showing a trend: use a line chart.
Showing parts of a whole: use a pie or stacked bar.
practices: Start the value axis at zero.
Sort bars by value unless the order is natural.
Use horizontal bars for long labels.
Label bars or provide a data table.

line-chart.what: A chart that connects points with lines to show how a value changes over time.
uses: Showing trends over days, months or years.
Comparing a value with an earlier period.
Spotting rises, falls and patterns.
avoid: A few unordered categories: use a bar chart.
More than a few series: split into smaller charts.
practices: Put time on the horizontal axis.
Limit to about four lines.
Vary line style as well as colour.
Label the lines directly or in a legend.

pie-chart.what: A circle divided into slices that show how a total splits into parts.
uses: Showing shares of a total.
Showing a simple split between a few groups.
Giving a quick overview of proportions.
avoid: More than five parts or close values: use a bar chart.
Comparing values over time: use a line chart.
practices: Keep to two to five slices.
Order slices from largest, starting at the top.
Show exact values or percentages in a legend.
Group small slices as 'Other'.

doughnut-chart.what: A pie chart with a hole in the middle, where the total or a key figure can be shown.
uses: Showing shares of a total with the total in the centre.
Showing progress toward a goal.
Giving a compact overview of a split.
avoid: More than five parts: use a bar chart.
Comparing values precisely: use a bar chart.
practices: Show the total in the centre.
Keep to a few slices.
Provide values in a legend or table.
Order slices by size.

scatter-chart.what: A chart that places points by two number values to show whether and how they are related.
uses: Checking whether two measures are related.
Spotting outliers in data.
Showing clusters of similar items.
avoid: One measure only: use a bar or line chart.
Time trends: use a line chart.
practices: Label both axes with units.
Use different marker shapes for groups.
Avoid too many points that overlap.
Mention any pattern in text.

bubble-chart.what: A scatter chart where the size of each point shows a third value.
uses: Comparing items across three measures.
Showing size alongside position, such as sales and share.
Spotting groups or outliers with weight.
avoid: Comparing exact sizes: use a table or bars.
Only two measures: use a scatter chart.
practices: Scale bubble area, not radius, to value.
Label the axes and what size means.
Keep the number of bubbles manageable.
Provide a table with exact values.

radar-chart.what: A chart that shows scores on several axes as a polygon, so the shape reveals strengths and gaps.
uses: Comparing one or two items across several criteria.
Showing a profile, such as skills or health scores.
Spotting weak areas at a glance.
avoid: More than two items: use a table or bars.
Criteria on different scales: use bars.
practices: Use the same scale on every axis.
Use four to eight axes.
Order axes in a meaningful way.
Provide a table for exact values.

polar-area-chart.what: A round chart with equal-angle segments, where each segment's distance from the centre shows its value.
uses: Showing counts across repeating categories, such as weekdays.
Giving a compact overview by type.
Comparing a handful of values in a round layout.
avoid: Precise comparisons: use a bar chart.
Parts of a whole: use a pie or doughnut chart.
practices: Order segments by time or size.
Label each segment.
Use a scale that starts at zero.
Provide a table with exact values.

logo.what: The symbol or wordmark that identifies a product or brand. It usually sits in a top bar or header and links to the home page.
uses: Showing the brand in the header or top bar.
Branding login and sign-up screens.
Branding emails and documents.
avoid: Repeating it many times on one screen.
Using it as decoration.
practices: Keep it in the same place on every page.
Link it to the home page.
Never stretch or recolour the file.
Give it the product name as alt text.

avatar.what: A small picture or set of initials that stands for a person, team or account.
uses: Showing who wrote a comment or made a change.
Listing people and team members.
Showing the signed-in user in a menu.
avoid: Decoration with no meaning.
Showing a company brand: use a logo.
practices: Show initials when there is no photo.
Keep the name nearby or in a tooltip.
Offer a few consistent sizes.
Give a text alternative when it stands alone.

favicon.what: The small icon that appears in browser tabs, bookmarks and on home screens to represent a site.
uses: Helping people find a tab among many.
Identifying a site in bookmarks and history.
Showing the app icon when saved to a home screen.
avoid: Showing the full brand: use a logo.
Detailed images that become unreadable when tiny.
practices: Keep it simple so it reads at 16px.
Provide an SVG or PNG and larger sizes for phones.
Make it clear on light and dark tabs.
Match it to the brand.
